tier_reason: Tier A rests on the independent LangArena suite: its benchmark code is public (c/src/log_parser.c with pcre2_jit_match, rust/src/benchmarks/log_parser.rs with regex::Regex::find_iter, the same 13 patterns and count-all-matches work). Its results file results/2026-10-05-kostya-ms7c37.js states the CPU (AMD Ryzen 7 3800X), clang 22.1.8, gcc 16.0.1 and rustc 1.99.0, and the C flags are in c/Makefile. rebar alone would be tier C: it is written by the regex crate's author, it lists engine versions but no CPU or compiler version, and its flags are only derivable from Cargo profiles.

corrections.claimed_speedup: rebar README summary of search-time benchmarks (geometric mean of per-benchmark speed ratios to the best engine, lower is better): hyperscan 2.37 (28 benchmarks), rust/regex 1.12.2 3.08 (38), pcre2/jit 10.47 6.00 (34), re2 10.39 (31), pcre2 interpreter 114.75 (33). The compile-time summary goes the other way: pcre2 1.41, pcre2/jit 6.20, rust/regex 11.85, re2 12.28. Intersection derived from the repo's recorded CSVs record/curated/2025-12-19/*.csv (median search times; derived from page data, re-computed by the verifier): vs PCRE2 JIT rust/regex is faster in 21 of 34 benchmarks, geometric-mean time ratio 2.13x; vs RE2 faster in 27 of 31, 4.3x; vs the PCRE2 interpreter faster in 32 of 33, 44x; vs Hyperscan faster in only 12 of 28 (Hyperscan about 1.45x faster overall). LangArena results 2026-10-05, Etc::LogParser (13 patterns, count all matches): Rust 0.302 s vs C with PCRE2 JIT 0.485 s (clang -O2), 0.488 s (gcc -O2) and 0.486 s (gcc -O3 -march=native 'Fast' build), about 1.6x; vs the C++ version, which uses RE2, 0.993-0.998 s (about 3.3x). In the same file, Template::Regex ({{(.*?)}} replacement): Rust 3.699 s vs C with PCRE2 JIT 1.155-1.173 s, so PCRE2 JIT is about 3.2x faster there; vs C++ RE2 4.84-4.90 s, Rust is about 1.3x faster.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: rebar: engine versions only (rust/regex 1.12.2, pcre2 10.47, re2 2025-11-05). PCRE2 (with SUPPORT_JIT) and RE2 are compiled from vendored source by the cc crate inside each engine's Cargo release profile (lto = fat, codegen-units = 1, default opt-level 3, so -O3 by the cc crate's default). This is derived from engines/pcre2/build.rs, engines/re2/build.rs and their Cargo.toml files; no compiler version is stated. LangArena: rustc 1.99.0, 'cargo build --release' with regex 1.12. C: clang 22.1.8 and gcc 16.0.1, prod flags -O2 -DNDEBUG -fstack-protector-strong -fno-omit-frame-pointer, Fast flags -O3 -march=native -mtune=native -funroll-loops with -flto=thin, linked against the system libpcre2-8. C++ is linked against the system libre2. The system PCRE2 and RE2 versions and build flags are not recorded in the results file.
corrections.hardware: rebar does not state the machine. LangArena results file: AMD Ryzen 7 3800X 8-Core Processor, 78 GB, x86_64 Linux.
corrections.caveats: rebar's summary geometric means cover different benchmark subsets per engine (28 to 38), so only the intersection numbers compare like for like; the verifier re-computed them from the repo's recorded CSVs and they match. rebar is written by the regex crate's author, and its README says the analysis is biased towards that crate (BIAS.md). rebar states no CPU or compiler version. Hyperscan beats regex overall, and PCRE2 JIT wins 13 of the 34 shared benchmarks. LangArena is independent, with public code, compilers, flags and CPU. Its C LogParser time is the same at -O2 and at -O3 -march=native (0.486 s), so the opt level does not explain the gap. The PCRE2 and RE2 it measures are system libraries whose versions and build flags are not recorded. The C++ LangArena rows use RE2, not PCRE2. LangArena's Template::Regex task shows a 3.2x loss to PCRE2 JIT. The win is a library and engine-design effect (lazy DFA plus SIMD literal prefilters), not a language effect.

notes: Every number checked: the rebar README summary tables, the intersection ratios re-computed from the 2025-12-19 CSVs (21/34 at 2.13x vs PCRE2 JIT, 27/31 at 4.3x vs RE2, 32/33 at 44x vs the PCRE2 interpreter, 12/28 at 0.69x vs Hyperscan) and the LangArena runtimes all match. Shortcomings: rebar is first-party and states no CPU; regex loses to Hyperscan overall, loses to PCRE2 JIT on about a third of rebar's benchmarks and on LangArena Template::Regex (3.2x); LangArena's baselines are system-packaged PCRE2 and RE2 with unrecorded versions and flags. Metadata confirmed: MIT OR Apache-2.0, 4.0k stars, last commit 2026-08-10. Not a duplicate: ripgrep (wave 11) is listed separately and uses this crate.

tier_reason: A WABI 2024 paper exists, but its headline numbers (19x, 5.6x, 0.81x) were seen only in a search snippet: drops.dagstuhl.de, bioRxiv and doi.org are blocked here. Under the wave-14 rule, snippet-only paper numbers stay at tier C. What could be opened is first-party: the README's 'up to 20x' sentence, and the pa-bench evals notebook (evals/astarpa2/evals.ipynb), whose saved output gives mean A*PA2-simple speedups over Edlib of 7.48 and 8.26 on synthetic data. Neither states a CPU model or compiler version.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Repo README: 'It achieves up to 20x speedup over other exact aligners and is competitive with approximate aligners' (the WABI paper title says 'up to 19x faster'). pa-bench evals/astarpa2/evals.ipynb saved output: mean speedup of A*PA2-simple over Edlib 7.48 on the scaling-n synthetic set and 8.26 on the scaling-e set (notebook output). Its runtime table, with a 'best A*PA2 vs best of Edlib/BiWFA' speedup row, has no saved output. Paper abstract, seen only in a search snippet (WABI 2024, LIPIcs 312; paper page blocked): 19x faster than BiWFA and Edlib on >500 kbp ONT reads with 6% divergence; 5.6x on 11 kbp reads with 11% divergence; 0.81x (slower) on 800 bp reads with 11% divergence.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: pa-bench release profile: lto = true, codegen-units = 1 (pa-bench Cargo.toml); A*PA2 is pulled in as a git dependency, and its repo pins a nightly toolchain (rust-toolchain.toml). The aligner repo's .cargo/config.toml sets -C target-cpu=native, but pa-bench does not state which RUSTFLAGS the paper runs used. Edlib is built by edlib-rs through the cmake crate; its build.rs passes '-D CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release' as a C flag, so the build type comes from the cmake crate's profile mapping (derived). The rust-wfa2 build for BiWFA was not checked.
corrections.hardware: CPU model not stated in pa-bench; evals/astarpa2/justfile pins the CPU at 3.6 GHz with cpupower (performance governor), and pa-bench pins each job to one core.
corrections.caveats: The paper's 19x, 5.6x and 0.81x figures are snippet only, because the LIPIcs and bioRxiv pages are blocked here. What could be opened is the author's own README claim and the pa-bench notebook. The full results live in a release results.zip that was not opened. No CPU model is stated in the repos. The speedup comes from a different algorithm: band doubling with Myers bit-packing plus blocks, SIMD, a new profile and the A* heuristics. It is not a Rust-vs-C++ language effect, and A*PA2 is slower than Edlib and BiWFA on short (800 bp) high-divergence reads. Pairwise alignment is on the edge of the string-and-text category.

notes: Downgraded from B to C: the peer-reviewed numbers could not be opened, and the reachable evidence (README, pa-bench notebook with 7.48x and 8.26x mean A*PA2-simple vs Edlib on synthetic data) is first-party with no CPU or compiler version. Shortcomings: algorithmic rather than language win; slower on short reads (0.81x, snippet); hardware unstated. Metadata confirmed: MPL-2.0, 152 stars, last commit 2026-05-22 (active).

tier_reason: lh3/biofast is an independent, well-known suite by the author of kseq.h, not of needletail. It has public code (fqcnt/fqcnt_rs2_needletail.rs, fqcnt/fqcnt_c1_kseq.c, fqcnt/Makefile), the C compiler and flags (gcc-4.8.5, -g -Wall -O2) and the CPU (2x EPYC 7301). The rustc version is not stated, so it falls short of A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: lh3/biofast README and fqcnt/README.md, fqcnt table (CPU seconds, hyperfine average): needletail plain 0.8 s vs C kseq.h 1.4 s (1.75x, derived from page data); gzip input 9.3 s vs 9.7 s (about equal, since decompression dominates). For reference, rust-bio in the same table is 2.4 s plain and 10.0 s gzip.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: C: gcc-4.8.5 with -g -Wall -O2 (fqcnt/Makefile), not -O3. Rust: 'cargo install' (release profile, default opt-level 3) with needletail = "0.4" (biofast Cargo.toml); rustc version not stated.
corrections.why_faster: A library-design effect, not a language one. needletail 0.4's parser is taken from seq_io (needletail README) and handles only FASTA and 4-line FASTQ, while kseq.h parses multi-line FASTA/FASTQ. The C program reads even plain input through zlib's gzopen/gzread pass-through. The C side is also built at -O2 with gcc-4.8.5 against a release Rust build.
corrections.caveats: This is an independent benchmark by the author of kseq.h, but it dates from 2020 and measured needletail 0.4 (the current README shows 0.6.0), so the numbers are stale. The C baseline is gcc-4.8.5 at -O2, not -O3. Plain-file C input still goes through zlib's gzread, and needletail handles only 4-line FASTQ against kseq.h's multi-line parser, which favours needletail. gzip input shows no gain (9.3 s vs 9.7 s). Needletail's own README claims only to aim to be 'as fast as the readfq C library' and has no benchmark section. The Crystal, Nim and Julia ports of kseq.h do not beat C in the same table.

notes: Numbers confirmed on lh3/biofast README and fqcnt/README.md (0.8 s vs 1.4 s plain, 9.3 s vs 9.7 s gzip). Shortcomings: stale 2020 run on needletail 0.4; C side gcc-4.8.5 -O2 rather than -O3; feature scope differs (4-line FASTQ only vs multi-line); C reads plain input through gzread; no gain on gzip input; the parser algorithm comes from seq_io. Metadata confirmed: MIT, 214 stars, last commit 2026-10-06 (active).
